How Bad Was It? Ipsos 2026 Among the Pre-Election Poll Misses of 2010–2026

A referenced catalogue of final-poll failures since 2010, and where the Ipsos Strategic Marketing poll for the Serbian parliamentary election of 25 October 2026 sits among them

Goran S. Milovanović, PhD

02 November 2026

# ---- a quiet ggplot theme ----------------------------------------------------
theme_report <- function(base_size = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#fcfcfb", colour = NA),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.4),
      axis.line.x      = element_line(colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 0.4),
      axis.ticks       = element_blank(),
      text             = element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
      plot.title       = element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", face = "bold", size = base_size + 2),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = "#52514e", size = base_size - 1),
      plot.caption     = element_text(colour = "#898781", size = base_size - 3, hjust = 0),
      legend.position  = "top",
      legend.title     = element_blank(),
      strip.text       = element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", face = "bold")
    )
}

fmt_n   <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "n/a", format(round(x), big.mark = ","))
fmt_pct <- function(x, d = 1) ifelse(is.na(x), "", sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x))
fmt_sgn <- function(x, d = 1) ifelse(is.na(x), "", sprintf(paste0("%+.", d, "f"), x))
# Serbian number formats (decimal comma)
fmt_d_sr <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ".", decimal.mark = ",")

# short agency label for charts: drop "(for …)" and other parentheticals
short_agency <- function(a, sr = FALSE) {
  a <- gsub(" \\([^)]*\\)", "", a)
  a <- sub("^Poll attributed to Ipsos Strategic Marketing$", if (sr) "pripisano Ipsosu SM" else "attributed to Ipsos SM", a)
  a <- sub("^ABC News / Washington Post$", "ABC News/WaPo", a)
  a
}

kable_report <- function(df, ..., align = NULL) {
  if (is.null(align)) {
    looks_num <- vapply(df, function(x) is.numeric(x) ||
                          all(grepl("^[-−+]?[0-9.,%× ]*$|<sup>|^$", as.character(x)) & !all(is.na(x)) & any(grepl("[0-9]", x))),
                        logical(1))
    align <- ifelse(looks_num, "r", "l")
  }
  kableExtra::kbl(df, ..., align = align, escape = FALSE) |>
    kableExtra::kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                              full_width = TRUE, position = "center")
}

Sažetak za javnost

Pitanje. Završna anketa agencije Ipsos Strategic Marketing (objavljena 22. oktobra 2026, n = 3.624) promašila je rezultat parlamentarnih izbora u Srbiji 25. oktobra 2026. za 13,0 poena na Studentskoj listi i 8,4 poena na listi Aleksandar Vučić – Ujedinjena Srbija, i to u pravcu koji je obrnuo pobednika. U prethodnom izveštaju pokazali smo da slučajna greška uzorka ne može da objasni taj promašaj. Ovde postavljamo drugo pitanje: koliko je ovaj promašaj veliki u poređenju sa najpoznatijim promašajima predizbornih anketa u svetu od 2010. godine?

Šta smo uradili. Sastavili smo katalog od 37 dobro dokumentovanih promašaja završnih predizbornih anketa (izbori i referendumi, 2010–2026, širom sveta), uključujući Brexit, američke izbore 2016. i 2020, britanske izbore 2015, 2017. i 2024, kolumbijski referendum o miru 2016, grčki referendum 2015, i anketu pripisanu Ipsosu pred drugi krug predsedničkih izbora u Srbiji 2012. (Tadić – Nikolić). Za svaki slučaj navodimo: šta je anketa objavila, šta su birači uradili, i šta su naknadne analize (zvanične istrage, naučni radovi, izjave samih agencija) ponudile kao objašnjenje. Svaki broj i svaka tvrdnja imaju referencu (odeljak References).

Kako merimo promašaj. Standardna mera u literaturi je greška razlike: koliko je anketa promašila razliku između pobednika i drugoplasiranog, u procentnim poenima. Na primer, Ipsos je 2026. imao Ujedinjenu Srbiju ispred Studentske liste za 7,4 poena; stvarna razlika bila je 14,0 poena u korist Studentske liste. Greška razlike je zato 7,4 + 14,0 = 21,4 poena. Pored toga računamo i standardizovanu grešku: grešku razlike podeljenu sa statističkom greškom koju bi slučajan uzorak te veličine imao — koliko „standardnih devijacija“ je anketa udaljena od istine. To je ista logika kao u prethodnom izveštaju, u pojednostavljenom obliku (dve liste umesto svih devetnaest).

Slika S1. Greška razlike (pobednik minus drugoplasirani, anketa minus rezultat) za svaki promašaj u katalogu, po apsolutnoj vrednosti. Narandžasto: Ipsos Strategic Marketing, Srbija (2026, i anketa iz 2012. pripisana Ipsosu). Plavo: druge Ipsos agencije. Sivo: ostale agencije. ✕ = anketa je imala pogrešnog pobednika. Prazan krug na redu 2012: alternativni izveštaj o istoj anketi (52/48).

Slika S2. Standardizovana greška: greška razlike podeljena standardnom greškom slučajnog uzorka te veličine. Prikazani su samo slučajevi za koje je veličina uzorka dokumentovana. Za Ipsos 2026. korišćena je efektivna veličina uzorka od 2.110, izvedena iz Ipsosovih sopstvenih objavljenih raspona greške (ne broj opredeljenih ispitanika, koji Ipsos nije objavio); to je izbor najpovoljniji za Ipsos. Prazan krug na redu 2026: vrednost sa nominalnih 3.624 ispitanika; na redu 2012: alternativni izveštaj (52/48).

Šta slike pokazuju.

  • Po sirovoj grešci razlike, Ipsos 2026. (21,4 poena) je 5. najveći promašaj u katalogu od 37 slučajeva i 3. najveći među izborima (za razliku od referenduma). Veći su: kolumbijski plebiscit o miru 2016. (Ipsos Napoleón Franco: 32,4 poena, izlaznost upola manja od pretpostavljene), grčki referendum 2015. (Public Issue: 22,1), i dve završne ankete pred drugi krug predsedničkih izbora u Kostariki 2018. — OPol (35,0; anketa koju je, kako se kasnije saznalo, naručio štab kandidata koji je izgubio) i nezavisni univerzitetski CIEP-UCR (22,2), u trci u kojoj je panel istog univerziteta posle izbora utvrdio da je 60% apstinenata iz prvog kruga glasalo za pobednika. Medijana promašaja ostalih redova — a to su redovi izabrani zato što su čuveni promašaji — iznosi 9,6 poena; Ipsos 2026. je 2,2 puta toliko.
  • Po standardizovanoj grešci — koja uzima u obzir da anketa od 3.600 ispitanika „nema pravo“ na grešku koju ima anketa od 600 — Ipsos 2026. je praktično izjednačen na 3. mestu sa Brazil 2022. (Datafolha) od 35 (z = 10,4 sa efektivnom veličinom uzorka od 2.110, izvedenom iz Ipsosovih objavljenih raspona greške; 13,6 sa nominalnih 3.624), u društvu: Kostarika 2018. (OPol Consultores), Argentina 2023. (AtlasIntel), Brazil 2022. (Datafolha), Bolivija 2020. (Ipsos). Slučajevi koji su, kao Ipsos 2026, u prvih pet i po sirovoj i po standardizovanoj meri: Kostarika 2018. (OPol Consultores).
  • Ipsos 2026. je takođe promašio pobednika, što je u katalogu slučaj u 51% redova, i promašio udeo Studentske liste za 13,0 poena — šest puta više od sopstvenog objavljenog raspona greške (±2,1 poena): stvarni udeo Studentske liste bio je 10,9 poena iznad gornje granice Ipsosovog intervala.
  • Ipsos nije bio usamljen, ali je među oktobarskim anketama bio najdalje. U oktobru 2026. samo je još jedna agencija objavila brojke: NSPM (terensko istraživanje 25. 9.–5. 10, n = 1.050, o sopstvenom trošku) imao je Studentsku listu ispred, 44,5 prema 42,7 — tačan pobednik, razlika potcenjena za 12 poena. Faktor plus (16.–20. 9, n = 986, naručilac nenaveden) imao je Ujedinjenu Srbiju ispred 48,6 prema 37,1 — promašaj od 25,5 poena, ali pet nedelja pred izbore. Procene CRTA-e (jun) i modela BIRODI (avgust) bile su u granicama pet poena od stvarne razlike. Ipsos je, dakle, anketa sa najsvežijim terenom i najvećim uzorkom; veću grešku imala je samo anketa Faktor plus, pet nedelja pred izbore (odeljak 3.5).
  • Najčešća objašnjenja u dokumentovanim istragama su: nereprezentativni uzorci koje ponderisanje nije popravilo (Velika Britanija 2015, Australija 2019), neodgovaranje i prikrivanje opredeljenja (SAD 2020, Turska 2023, Argentina 2019), modeli izlaznosti i sastav biračkog tela (Kolumbija, Kostarika, Čile, Bolivija), kasni preokret (Alberta 2012, Brazil 2022, Holandija 2023). Nijedno od ovih objašnjenja statistika sama ne može da potvrdi ni za Ipsos 2026; to zahteva Ipsosove sirove podatke. Prikrivanje opredeljenja je, treba reći, mehanizam koji bi delovao u smeru koji je i zabeležen (telefonska anketa u polarizovanoj kampanji, potcenjena opozicija) — ali u dokumentovanim slučajevima proizvodi 5–10 poena, ne 21, i ne objašnjava zašto je svih šesnaest malih lista precenjeno. Ono što katalog pokazuje jeste da među izbornim anketama sa terenom u poslednjoj nedelji, uzorkom od dve hiljade i više, objavljenim naručiocem i neosporenim rezultatom, promašaj ove veličine nema parnjaka u ovom katalogu.

Srbija 2012. Deset dana pred drugi krug predsedničkih izbora (20. maj 2012), mediji su objavili istraživanje pripisano Ipsos Strategic Marketingu (terensko istraživanje 10. maja, n = 1.198): Tadić 58%, Nikolić 42%; drugi izveštaj iz istih dana navodi 52 prema 48. Nikolić je pobedio sa 51,2% prema 48,8% važećih glasova. Ipsos je naknadno (2021, 2022) saopštio da nikakve brojke za drugi krug nije zvanično objavio, da sopstveno istraživanje za drugi krug nije ni imao, i da je neko medijima dao podatke pod imenom Ipsosa; to je u tabeli i referencama navedeno, a obe verzije brojki prikazane su na graficima. Sa objavljenih 58/42, greška razlike je 18,3 poena; sa 52/48, 6,3.

Potpuna analiza, tabela sa svim slučajevima i reference slede na engleskom.

1 Introduction

1.1 The question

On 25 October 2026 Serbia held snap parliamentary elections. The final pre-election poll by Ipsos Strategic Marketing, published on 22 October (fieldwork 20–22 October, n = 3,624, commissioned by the Ujedinjena Srbija list), had Aleksandar Vučić – Ujedinjena Srbija at 47.4% and Studentska lista – Studenti pobeđuju at 40.0%, with a stated margin of ±2.1 points.1 The Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) counted Studentska lista 53.0%, Ujedinjena Srbija 39.0%.2

The companion technical report establishes that random sampling error cannot account for this: the exact multinomial probability of a random sample landing at least that far from the truth is about 2 × 10−36, and no variant of the assumptions lifts it above 10−30.3 That report deliberately says nothing about why the gap exists.

This document asks a different, comparative question: how large is the 2026 Ipsos miss relative to the well-documented pre-election polling failures of the last sixteen years, worldwide? Polls miss. The literature on polling error is large, and the misses that entered the public memory — the 2015 British general election, the Brexit referendum, the US state polls of 2016 and 2020, Israel 2015, Australia 2019, the Colombian peace plebiscite — each produced inquiries and post-mortems. Putting Ipsos 2026 next to them, on a common scale, is the only way to say whether “polls miss sometimes” is an adequate description of what happened.

1.2 What this document does and does not do

Read this before reading any number below.

  1. Scope. Final pre-election polls (published before the vote), for national or sub-national elections and referendums, worldwide, from 2010 to 2026. Exit polls, seat projections built from constituency models, and forecasting aggregators are out of scope, with one exception noted in the table (the Brexit poll of polls is reported alongside individual polls for context). Three further rules. (a) Only polls whose fieldwork ended within 16 days of the vote — the longest legal pre-election blackout among the cases (Chile) — count as final polls; an agency’s last poll published five weeks out is not a final poll and is reported in the text, not the table. (b) The official count is taken as the truth, because the metric has no other anchor; elections whose official count is disputed by international observers (Venezuela 2024, Georgia 2024) are therefore excluded and listed in Section 4 with their figures. (c) A case enters the catalogue when the final poll(s) either got the winner wrong, or missed the margin between the top two by at least about five points. The five-point threshold is this document’s own choice, not a figure from the literature; it is roughly twice the typical final-week error on a party share reported by Jennings & Wlezien (about 2 points), and large enough that every case in the British, American and Australian inquiries clears it.4
  2. One row per poll, not per election. Where an election had many pollsters, the table lists the final poll(s) most cited in the post-mortems, so that a named agency with a published sample size can be compared with a named agency. Poll averages, where an official one exists, are mentioned in the text but are not rows.
  3. Sourcing. Every poll figure is referenced to the agency’s own release or, where that is no longer online, to a contemporaneous report of it; every official result to the electoral authority or a document reproducing its figures; every explanation to the inquiry, academic paper, pollster statement or press analysis that offered it, labelled by type. Where only a secondary source could be reached, the table says so. All links were checked on 2 November 2026.
  4. What the catalogue cannot show. It cannot say why Ipsos 2026 missed. The explanations column records what others concluded about their misses; it is context, not diagnosis. The document makes no claim about intent in any case.
  5. It is not exhaustive. Candidate cases that were considered and left out, and why, are listed in Section 4.

1.3 How a miss is measured

1.3.0.1 Concept: margin error and standardised error

The measure used here is the error on the margin: take the eventual winner and the eventual runner-up (or the winning and losing option in a referendum), compute the poll’s lead for the winner, compute the actual lead, and subtract. It is the headline measure of the AAPOR task-force reports on the 2016 and 2020 US polls, and one of the two measures in Jennings & Wlezien’s comparative study of 351 elections, whose primary measure is the absolute error on each party’s share.4,51

\[E = (\hat{p}_{\text{winner}} - \hat{p}_{\text{runner-up}}) - (p_{\text{winner}} - p_{\text{runner-up}})\]

where \(\hat{p}\) are the polled shares and \(p\) the official shares. A negative \(E\) means the poll underestimated the winner’s lead; \(E\) below \(-(p_{\text{winner}} - p_{\text{runner-up}})\) means the poll had the wrong winner. This measure is used because it is what readers of a poll actually act on (who is ahead, and by how much), and because it is insensitive to how undecided respondents or small parties are treated, as long as the two leading options are measured on the same base.

A raw error of five points means different things for a poll of 600 respondents and a poll of 3,600. A random sample of size \(n\) from a population in which the two leading options have shares \(p_1, p_2\) produces a lead whose standard error is

\[\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{p_1 + p_2 - (p_1 - p_2)^2}{n}}\]

(the variance of a difference of two multinomial proportions). The standardised error \(z = |E| / \text{SE}\) is the number of standard errors by which the poll missed, under the hypothesis that it was a simple random sample of the voting population. It is the two-category version of the test in the companion report, and is reported only where the poll’s sample size is documented. Under random sampling, \(|z| > 2\) happens about one time in twenty; \(|z| > 4\) about one time in 16,000; \(|z| > 6\) about one time in 500 million.

refs <- refs |> dplyr::mutate(num = dplyr::row_number())
ref_num <- setNames(refs$num, refs$id)
# inline citation: cite("uk15_ipsos", "uk15_result") -> <sup>11,12</sup> with anchors
cite <- function(...) {
  ids <- unlist(strsplit(paste(c(...), collapse = ";"), ";"))
  stopifnot(all(ids %in% names(ref_num)))
  paste0("<sup>", paste(sprintf('<a href="#ref-%s">%d</a>', ids, ref_num[ids]), collapse = ","), "</sup>")
}

2.2 The catalogue

Each row is one final pre-election poll. poll_w / poll_r are the polled shares of the eventual winner and runner-up (or winning and losing referendum option); act_w / act_r the official shares; n the poll’s sample size as published (NA where no primary or contemporaneous source states it). Shares are on the base the poll itself used (decided voters, valid votes, two-party-preferred, …) and the official result is taken on the same base wherever the sources allow; the basis column says which. For Israel 2015, where polls report seats, polled “shares” are seat shares (seats / 120).

  dplyr::mutate(
    date   = as.Date(date),
    year   = as.integer(format(date, "%Y")),
    poll_lead   = poll_w - poll_r,
    actual_lead = act_w - act_r,
    E           = poll_lead - actual_lead,            # margin error, points (negative = winner underestimated)
    absE        = abs(E),
    wrong_winner = poll_lead < 0,
    pw = act_w / 100, pr = act_r / 100,
    se_margin = 100 * sqrt((pw + pr - (pw - pr)^2) / n),  # SE of the polled lead under random sampling, points
    z = absE / se_margin
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date, agency) |>
  dplyr::mutate(no = dplyr::row_number())
tbl <- misses |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Event = sprintf("<b>%s</b><br><span style='color:#52514e'>%s · %s</span>", event, format(date, "%d %b %Y"), type),
    n_label = ifelse(id == "rs26", "n = 3,624 published; n<sub>eff</sub> = 2,110 derived", paste0("n = ", fmt_n(n))),
    Agency = sprintf("<b>%s</b>%s<br><span style='color:#52514e'>%s · %s · %s · %s</span>",
                     agency,
                     purrr::map_chr(poll_refs, ~ cite(.x)),
                     fieldwork, mode, n_label, basis),
    Poll = sprintf("%s <b>%s</b><br>%s %s<br><span style='color:#52514e'>lead %s</span>",
                   winner, fmt_pct(poll_w), runner, fmt_pct(poll_r), fmt_sgn(poll_lead)),
    Result = sprintf("%s <b>%s</b><br>%s %s<br><span style='color:#52514e'>lead %s</span>%s",
                     winner, fmt_pct(act_w), runner, fmt_pct(act_r), fmt_sgn(actual_lead),
                     purrr::map_chr(result_refs, ~ cite(.x))),
    Miss = sprintf("<b>%s</b> pts%s<br><span style='color:#52514e'>z = %s</span>",
                   fmt_sgn(E), ifelse(wrong_winner, "<br><span style='color:#eb6834'>wrong winner</span>", ""),
                   ifelse(is.na(z), "n/a", sprintf("%.1f", z))),
    Explanation = sprintf("%s%s%s", explanation, purrr::map_chr(expl_refs, ~ cite(.x)),
                          ifelse(caveat == "", "", sprintf("<br><span style='color:#898781'><i>%s</i></span>", caveat)))
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(`#` = no, Event, Agency, `Poll (final)` = Poll, `Official result` = Result, `Margin error` = Miss, `Possible explanation (type: source)` = Explanation)

kable_report(tbl, align = c("r", "l", "l", "l", "l", "r", "l"),
             caption = sprintf("Table 1. %d final pre-election poll misses, 2010–2026, in chronological order. Margin error = (polled lead of the eventual winner) − (actual lead); negative means the winner was underestimated. z = |margin error| / standard error of the lead for a random sample of the poll's size (see Section 1.3); n/a where the sample size is not documented. Superscripts link to the numbered references.", nrow(misses))) |>

  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "13em") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(3, width = "15em") |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(4, width = "10em") |>

Table 1. 37 final pre-election poll misses, 2010–2026, in chronological order. Margin error = (polled lead of the eventual winner) − (actual lead); negative means the winner was underestimated. z = |margin error| / standard error of the lead for a random sample of the poll’s size (see Section 1.3); n/a where the sample size is not documented. Superscripts link to the numbered references.
# Event Agency Poll (final) Official result Margin error Possible explanation (type: source)
1 Alberta (Canada) provincial election
23 Apr 2012 · Election 		Forum Research56
22 Apr 2012 · IVR telephone · n = n/a · decided or leaning, certain to vote 		Progressive Conservatives 36.0
Wildrose 38.0
lead -2.0 		Progressive Conservatives 44.0
Wildrose 34.3
lead +9.757 		-11.7 pts
wrong winner
z = n/a 		Pollster (ThinkHQ): its own tracking saw the Wildrose lead fall from 13 to 8 points within four or five days as Liberal and NDP supporters shifted to the PCs after the “conscience rights” controversies; most media polls stop three or four days before the vote.58
Forum’s election-eve poll is known only through press reports (no sample size). Its 21 April poll (n = 2,010) had Wildrose 41, PC 32, as did Angus Reid’s — a margin error of −18.7; the table uses the agency’s actual final poll.
2 Serbia presidential election, 2nd round (Tadić–Nikolić)
20 May 2012 · Election 		Poll attributed to Ipsos Strategic Marketing11,12
10 May 2012 · not stated · n = 1,198 · two-candidate split, base not stated 		Nikolić 42.0
Tadić 58.0
lead -16.0 		Nikolić 51.2
Tadić 48.8
lead +2.313 		-18.3 pts
wrong winner
z = 6.3 		Pollster (Ipsos, 2021 and 2022): Ipsos did not officially publish runoff figures and had no runoff survey of its own; data it collected for a client in 2012 mostly showed a tight race; someone gave media data under Ipsos’s name. Tadić’s loss is attributed to an equal opponent, DS exhaustion after the first round, a weak runoff campaign, low Belgrade turnout and the blank-ballot campaign; a demobilising effect of the reported poll is offered as speculation. Press (2012): agency estimates of an 8–16-point Tadić lead, two weeks of DS triumphalism, and the election-theft narrative keeping some voters at home.14,15,16
Two contemporaneous reports give different figures: 58/42 (Al Jazeera Balkans, with n and fieldwork date) and 52/48 (AP, a week later, no n). The table uses 58/42 because it is the report with methodology and the figure that entered the public record; with 52/48 the margin error is −6.3 (shown as a hollow point in the charts). No Ipsos release exists and Ipsos disputes authorship. Result on valid votes (RIK’s shares of all ballots: 49.54/47.31).
3 Kenya presidential election, 1st round
04 Mar 2013 · Election 		Ipsos Synovate129
15–19 Feb 2013 · face-to-face (as compiled) · n = 5,971 · all respondents incl. 3% undecided; result on all ballots 		Kenyatta 44.8
Odinga 44.4
lead +0.4 		Kenyatta 50.1
Odinga 43.3
lead +6.8130 		-6.4 pts
z = 5.1 		Pollster: Ipsos’s own post-election analysis found every candidate within the margin except Kenyatta, who outperformed the final poll by 5.25 points; attributed to differential turnout in the candidates’ strongholds (about 88–90% vs 84%).131
Sample size, dates and mode rest on a compiled table; fieldwork closed 13 days before the vote. Later polls had Odinga ahead and missed by more (Infotrak 45/46: −7.8).
4 British Columbia (Canada) provincial election
14 May 2013 · Election 		Ipsos Reid52
13 May 2013 · online panel · n = 800 · decided voters 		BC Liberals 37.0
BC NDP 45.0
lead -8.0 		BC Liberals 44.1
BC NDP 39.7
lead +4.453 		-12.4 pts
wrong winner
z = 3.8 		Pollster (Ipsos): 23% of voters decided in the final week and broke 41–34 for the Liberals; NDP supporters did not turn out. Pollster (Angus Reid, whose final poll had NDP 45, Liberals 36): under-35s weighted to about 30% of the population rather than about 15% of actual voters; correcting this alone would have cut the NDP lead to about three points; its follow-up found no late switching.54,55
The two pollsters give incompatible diagnoses of the same miss. Angus Reid’s final poll (margin error −13.4) is not a separate row because its fieldwork dates could not be established from a primary source.

rs26 <- misses |> dplyr::filter(id == "rs26")
rank_abs   <- misses |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(absE)) |> dplyr::mutate(r = dplyr::row_number())
rank_abs_e <- misses |> dplyr::filter(type == "Election") |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(absE)) |> dplyr::mutate(r = dplyr::row_number())
rank_z     <- misses |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(z)) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(z)) |> dplyr::mutate(r = dplyr::row_number())
r26_abs   <- rank_abs$r[rank_abs$id == "rs26"]
r26_abs_e <- rank_abs_e$r[rank_abs_e$id == "rs26"]
r26_z     <- rank_z$r[rank_z$id == "rs26"]
z26_nominal <- rs26$absE / (100 * sqrt((rs26$pw + rs26$pr - (rs26$pw - rs26$pr)^2) / 3624))
med_abs <- median(misses$absE[misses$id != "rs26"])
share_wrong <- mean(misses$wrong_winner)
ordinal <- function(k) paste0(k, c("th","st","nd","rd",rep("th",6))[ifelse(k %% 100 %in% 11:13, 1, k %% 10 + 1)])
top5_abs_ids <- rank_abs$id[rank_abs$r <= 5]
top5_z_ids   <- rank_z$id[rank_z$r <= 5]
both_top5    <- setdiff(intersect(top5_abs_ids, top5_z_ids), "rs26")
case_name    <- function(ids) { d <- misses[match(ids, misses$id), ]; sprintf("%s %d (%s)", d$country, d$year, short_agency(d$agency)) }
case_name_sr <- function(ids) { d <- misses[match(ids, misses$id), ]; sprintf("%s %d. (%s)", country_sr[d$country], d$year, short_agency(d$agency, sr = TRUE)) }
both_top5_txt <- if (length(both_top5)) paste(case_name(both_top5), collapse = " and ") else "none"
both_top5_sr  <- if (length(both_top5)) paste(case_name_sr(both_top5), collapse = " i ") else "nijedan"
top5_z_others <- setdiff(top5_z_ids, "rs26")
n_above15 <- sum(misses$absE > 15)
# alternative readings shown as hollow points: Serbia 2012 with the AP report (52/48); Serbia 2026 with the nominal n
rs12 <- misses |> dplyr::filter(id == "rs12")
E12_alt <- (48 - 52) - (rs12$act_w - rs12$act_r)
alt_pts <- tibble::tibble(id = c("rs12", "rs26"), E_alt = c(E12_alt, rs26$E), z_alt = c(abs(E12_alt) / rs12$se_margin, z26_nominal))
# rank text that admits ties within 0.1
z_near <- rank_z |> dplyr::filter(id != "rs26", abs(z - rs26$z) < 0.1)
z_rank_txt <- if (nrow(z_near)) sprintf("effectively tied for %s with %s", ordinal(min(r26_z, z_near$r)), paste(case_name(z_near$id), collapse = " and ")) else ordinal(r26_z)
z_rank_sr  <- if (nrow(z_near)) sprintf("praktično izjednačen na %d. mestu sa %s", min(r26_z, z_near$r), paste(case_name_sr(z_near$id), collapse = " i ")) else sprintf("%d.", r26_z)

3 The comparison

3.1 Raw margin error

plot_df <- misses |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = sprintf("%s %d · %s", country, year, short_agency(agency)),
    label = ifelse(wrong_winner, paste0(label, " ✕"), label),
    label = forcats::fct_reorder(label, absE),
    agency_group = factor(agency_group, levels = names(col)[1:3])
  )

ggplot(plot_df, aes(y = label)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = E, yend = label, colour = agency_group), linewidth = 1.6, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_point(aes(x = E, colour = agency_group), size = 3.4) +
  geom_point(data = plot_df |> dplyr::inner_join(alt_pts |> dplyr::filter(id == "rs12"), by = "id"), aes(x = E_alt), shape = 21, size = 3.4, colour = col[1], fill = "white", stroke = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-5, 5), colour = "#c3c2b7", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col[1:3]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-35, 20, 5), labels = function(x) ifelse(x == 0, "0", sprintf("%+d", x))) +
  labs(x = "Margin error, points (polled lead of the eventual winner minus actual lead)", y = NULL,
       title = "How far the final poll missed the winner's margin",
       subtitle = sprintf("%d final pre-election polls, 2010–2026. Dashed lines: ±5 points. ✕ = wrong winner.", nrow(misses))) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9.5), legend.position = "top")

Figure 1. Margin error of every poll in the catalogue, ranked by absolute value. Dot position is the signed error (negative: the eventual winner was underestimated); the bar length is its absolute value. Orange: Ipsos Strategic Marketing, Serbia (2026, and the 2012 poll attributed to it). Blue: other Ipsos entities. Grey: other agencies. Rows marked ✕ had the wrong winner. The hollow point on the 2012 row is the alternative contemporaneous report of that poll (52/48). Median absolute error of the other 36 rows: 9.6 points.

3.2 Standardised error

plot_z <- plot_df |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(z)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = forcats::fct_reorder(label, z))
nominal_pt <- plot_z |> dplyr::inner_join(alt_pts, by = "id") |> dplyr::mutate(z = z_alt)

ggplot(plot_z, aes(y = label)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 2, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#e1e0d9", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = z, yend = label, colour = agency_group), linewidth = 1.6, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_point(aes(x = z, colour = agency_group), size = 3.4) +
  geom_point(data = nominal_pt, aes(x = z), shape = 21, size = 3.4, colour = col[1], fill = "white", stroke = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col[1:3]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 22, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Standardised error (standard errors of a random sample of the poll's size)", y = NULL,
       title = "The same misses, scaled by what sampling error could produce",
       subtitle = "Larger samples have less excuse: a 5-point miss is z ≈ 2.5 at n = 600 and z ≈ 10 at n = 9,500.\nGrey band: z ≤ 2. Hollow points: Ipsos 2026 with the nominal n = 3,624; Serbia 2012 on the 52/48 report.") +
  theme_report() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9.5), legend.position = "top")

Figure 2. Standardised error: the absolute margin error divided by the standard error of the polled lead for a simple random sample of the poll’s published size. Only polls with a documented sample size are shown. The grey band marks z ≤ 2, the range an honest random sample stays within 19 times out of 20. For Ipsos 2026 the effective sample size of 2,110 is used (the choice most favourable to Ipsos); the hollow point on the 2026 row shows the value with the nominal n = 3,624, and on the 2012 row the value for the alternative report (52/48).

3.3 What the comparison shows

top_abs <- rank_abs |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 8) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Rank = r, Case = sprintf("%s %d · %s", country, year, agency), Type = type,
                   `Margin error` = fmt_sgn(E), z = ifelse(is.na(z), "n/a", sprintf("%.1f", z)))
top_z <- rank_z |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 8) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Rank = r, Case = sprintf("%s %d · %s", country, year, agency), n = fmt_n(n),
                   `Margin error` = fmt_sgn(E), z = sprintf("%.1f", z))
kable_report(top_abs, caption = "Table 2. The eight largest misses by raw margin error.")

Table 3. The eight largest misses by standardised error (documented sample sizes only).
Rank Case n Margin error z
1 Costa Rica 2018 · OPol Consultores 3,300 -35.0 20.6
2 Argentina 2023 · AtlasIntel 9,517 -13.0 16.6
3 Brazil 2022 · Datafolha 12,800 +8.8 10.4
4 Serbia 2026 · Ipsos Strategic Marketing 2,110 -21.4 10.4
5 Bolivia 2020 · Ipsos (for RTP) 2,000 -18.8 9.6
6 United Kingdom 2016 · Populus 4,740 -13.8 9.5
7 Paraguay 2023 · AtlasIntel 2,320 -16.3 9.5
8 Colombia 2016 · Ipsos Napoleón Franco (for Semana/RCN) 851 -32.4 9.5

Where Ipsos 2026 sits. With a margin error of -21.4 points, the Ipsos Strategic Marketing poll of 22 October 2026 is the 5th-largest miss in a catalogue of 37 documented final-poll failures from 16 years and 23 countries, and the 3rd-largest among elections (as opposed to referendums). Above it are two referendums in which the situation changed between fieldwork and the vote — the Colombian peace plebiscite of 2016 (Ipsos Napoleón Franco, −32.4, turnout half of what the polls assumed) and the Greek bailout referendum of 2015 (Public Issue, -22.1) — and the two final polls of the Costa Rican presidential runoff of 2018: OPol (-35.0, a poll commissioned by the losing candidate’s campaign, which was not disclosed at the time) and the independent CIEP-UCR (-22.2), in a race where the university’s own panel study later found that 60% of first-round abstainers had turned out for the winner. The median absolute margin error of the other 36 rows — rows selected because they are famous misses — is 9.6 points; Ipsos 2026 is 2.2 times that.

On the standardised scale it is effectively tied for 3rd with Brazil 2022 (Datafolha) of 35 with the effective sample size of 2,110 (z = 10.4), and 3rd with the nominal 3,624 (z = 13.6). The other cases in the top five on both scales: Costa Rica 2018 (OPol Consultores).

Three readings of the two charts.

First, the raw scale. Most of the catalogue sits between 5 and 14 points. That band contains the misses that produced formal inquiries — the 2015 British election (−5.6 for Ipsos MORI, −6.6 for the average), Brexit (−7.8 for Ipsos MORI and the poll of polls, −13.8 for Populus), Australia 2019 (−6.1), the 2016 Wisconsin polls (−6.8), Israel 2015 (−8.4). The inquiries treated errors of this size as serious institutional failures: the British Polling Council and the Market Research Society commissioned an independent panel after 2015, AAPOR convened committees after 2016 and 2020, the Australian industry body held an inquiry after 2019.19,51,134 Above 15 points there are 9 rows. Apart from Ipsos 2026, each carries a visible explanation in its post-mortem: an electorate that changed shape between fieldwork and the vote (a turnout collapse in Colombia, a 28% undeclared bloc in Bolivia, the consolidation of the field and of first-round abstainers behind the winner in Costa Rica), capital controls imposed on the eve of fieldwork (Greece), a single online pollster at odds with every other poll in the race (Paraguay), a ten-day-old poll of disputed provenance (Serbia 2012), or a single outlier poll that still had the winner right (ABC/WaPo in Wisconsin 2020, where the average missed by 6). Ipsos 2026 has none of these on its face: fieldwork ended three days before the vote, the poll was the agency’s own, it had the wrong winner, and — as Section 3.5 shows — the one independent survey published in the same month had the right one.

Second, the standardised scale. Dividing by the sampling standard error does two things. It pulls the large-sample polls to the top (OPol in Costa Rica at n = 3,300, AtlasIntel in Argentina 2023 at n = 9,517, Datafolha at n = 12,800), which is the point: a big sample buys precision, not accuracy, and a 9–35-point miss on a sample that size is a bias of ten standard errors or more. And it drops the small-sample misses of the US Senate races, British Columbia and the 2015 Ipsos MORI poll (n = 556–1,186) to z ≈ 1.5–4 — a different order of failure, and a reminder that the standardised scale is blind to the thing the British and Australian inquiries actually found: a bias that was small in any one poll but identical across all of them (pooling Australia’s 17 final polls gives n ≈ 23,600 and a z of about 9).135 Ipsos 2026, at z = 10.4 even on the Ipsos-friendliest sample size, is in the first group. This is the two-category shadow of the companion report’s result: there, with all lists and the exact multinomial tail, the equivalent figure is about 12 standard deviations on Studentska lista alone and a tail probability of 10−36.3

Third, what the post-mortems found, and what that does and does not say about 2026. The explanations column converges on a short list, and it is worth stating what each would require here.

  • Unrepresentative samples that weighting did not fix (UK 2015, Australia 2019, Brexit’s education gap, AAPOR 2016 on state polls).19,134,25,48 These produced errors of 3–7 points on the margin. To produce 21 points by this route, the sample would have to be skewed on a scale the inquiries never found.
  • Non-response and concealment correlated with the vote (AAPOR 2020; KONDA 2023; the Argentine “voto vergüenza”; Israel 2015).51,93,108,65 This is the mechanism a defender of the 2026 poll would reach for first, and it is directionally consistent with what happened: in a 90%-telephone survey conducted under a polarised campaign, opposition supporters declining to answer or to declare would under-measure Studentska lista. The documented cases cut both ways on who is under-declared — the incumbent in the US 2020, Turkey 2023 and Israel 2015; the opposition in Argentina 2019 and Slovakia 2023 — and the documented magnitudes are 5–10 points on the margin. Producing 21 would require concealment on a scale none of these post-mortems found, and it would not by itself explain why sixteen small lists were all overestimated.
  • Late swing after fieldwork (Alberta 2012, Brazil 2022, Netherlands 2023, Hungary 2022).58,117,84,77 The companion report puts a number on this: about 450,000 voters would have had to move to Studentska lista between 22 and 25 October for the poll to be an ordinary unlucky draw, and such a swing would not explain why the small lists were all overestimated in the same direction.3
  • Turnout and the composition of the electorate (Colombia, Costa Rica, Chile, Bolivia, Brexit).96,102,124,128,25 The misses in this group are the largest in the catalogue, and each involved a turnout the pollsters had not modelled or an undecided share above 15%; the case closest in size to Ipsos 2026 (Costa Rica 2018) is of exactly this kind. It is therefore the mechanism that deserves the most careful statement for Serbia. Turnout was 68.9% against 58.8% at the previous parliamentary election of December 2023 — about 620,000 more voters on a slightly smaller register — and against the 64.7% Ipsos itself expected.2,10,1 The relevant counterfactual for the poll is its own turnout model: relative to it, about 275,000 more people voted than Ipsos expected, and the companion report’s Scenario 3 shows that even if every one of them had voted for Studentska lista, a further 300,000 of the voters Ipsos did sample would still have had to switch.3 A composition change on the Costa Rican or Colombian scale would have required a turnout error of ten points or more; Ipsos’s was four.
  • Herding and polls published too early (UK 2015, Australia 2019, Czechia, Peru).19,135,87,121 Not applicable in form: Ipsos was the last poll, three days out, and the only other October survey pointed the other way.

None of this identifies the cause of the 2026 miss, and this document does not try to. What the catalogue establishes is narrower: among election polls with fieldwork in the final week, from samples of two thousand or more, with a disclosed commissioning party and an undisputed count, an error of this size has no counterpart in this catalogue. The two election misses that exceed it (Costa Rica 2018) were published 11–16 days before a runoff in which the field consolidated behind the winner, and the larger of them was commissioned by the losing campaign without disclosure. Resolving which, if any, of the mechanisms above operated in Serbia requires what every serious inquiry in the catalogue began by requesting: the raw data, the weighting scheme, the likely-voter model and the treatment of undecided respondents.19,134

3.4 Serbia 2012 and 2026, side by side

misses |> dplyr::filter(country == "Serbia") |>
  dplyr::transmute(Year = year, Event = event, Poll = sprintf("%s %s – %s %s", winner, fmt_pct(poll_w), runner, fmt_pct(poll_r)),
                   Result = sprintf("%s %s – %s %s", winner, fmt_pct(act_w), runner, fmt_pct(act_r)),
                   `Margin error` = fmt_sgn(E), n = fmt_n(n), z = sprintf("%.1f", z),
                   `Days from fieldwork to vote` = c(10, 3)) |>
  kable_report(caption = "Table 4. The two Serbian cases. For 2012 the figures are those reported by Al Jazeera Balkans; with the AP report (52/48) the margin error is −6.3.")
Table 4. The two Serbian cases. For 2012 the figures are those reported by Al Jazeera Balkans; with the AP report (52/48) the margin error is −6.3.
Year Event Poll Result Margin error n z Days from fieldwork to vote
2012 Serbia presidential election, 2nd round (Tadić–Nikolić) Nikolić 42.0 – Tadić 58.0 Nikolić 51.2 – Tadić 48.8 -18.3 1,198 6.3 10
2026 Serbia parliamentary election Studentska lista 40.0 – Ujedinjena Srbija 47.4 Studentska lista 53.0 – Ujedinjena Srbija 39.0 -21.4 2,110 10.4 3

The 2012 case is included on the figures reported at the time (Tadić 58, Nikolić 42; fieldwork 10 May, n = 1,198) because those are the figures that circulated under Ipsos’s name and entered the public record as “Ipsos missed in 2012”.11,16 They are the only version with a sample size and a fieldwork date; a second contemporaneous report gives 52/48, which would reduce the margin error to −6.3, and both are shown in the charts.12 Ipsos’s own account, given in 2021 and 2022, is that it did not officially publish any runoff figures, that it had no runoff survey of its own, that data it collected for a client that year mostly showed a tight race, and that someone gave media data under its name.14,15 That account cannot be checked against a release, because none exists. Either way the two Serbian rows differ in kind: in 2012 a disputed poll ten days out had a 16-point lead collapse in a low-turnout runoff; in 2026 the poll was Ipsos’s own, published three days out with a stated margin of ±2.1, and the Studentska lista share alone missed by 13.0 points, six times that margin (the 95% margin on the lead, for the implied sample size, is about ±4 points, and the lead missed by 21, roughly five such margins).

3.5 The other Serbian polls of 2026

A single poll can be an outlier or part of a pattern, and the two are judged differently: the Wisconsin 2020 poll was one firm’s outlier against an average that missed by 6; the British polls of 2015 all missed together. Which was Ipsos 2026? In October 2026 exactly one other agency published voting-intention figures, and three earlier estimates exist.9

rik_lead <- rs26$act_w - rs26$act_r
other_rs <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Source, ~Published, ~Fieldwork, ~n, ~Base, ~SL, ~US, ~refs,
  "NSPM (own expense)",                 "20 Oct 2026", "25 Sep–5 Oct 2026", 1050, "decided voters (18.3% undecided excluded)", 44.5, 42.7, "rs26_nspm",
  "Ipsos Strategic Marketing (for the Ujedinjena Srbija list)", "22 Oct 2026", "20–22 Oct 2026", 3624, "decided voters, incl. 2.5% assumed invalid", 40.0, 47.4, "rs26_ipsos",
  "Faktor plus (commissioner not stated; via Blic)", "21 Sep 2026", "16–20 Sep 2026", 986, "those who would vote", 37.1, 48.6, "rs26_faktor",
  "CRTA / Stanford DAL (own)",          "15 Jul 2026", "10–24 Jun 2026", 2324, "decided voters, face-to-face", 44.9, 35.7, "rs26_crta",
  "BIRODI forecast model (not a survey)", "30 Aug 2026", "model on RIK results and published polls", NA, "valid votes", 48.5, 38.6, "rs26_birodi"
) |> dplyr::mutate(E = (SL - US) - rik_lead,
                   days = c(20, 3, 35, 123, NA))
other_rs |>
  dplyr::transmute(Source = paste0(Source, purrr::map_chr(refs, cite)), Published, Fieldwork, n = fmt_n(n), Base,

Every estimate understated Studentska lista’s lead, so 2026 is not a lone-outlier case; but the magnitudes separate sharply. The civic-sector estimates (CRTA in June, the BIRODI model in August) were within five points of the eventual margin. NSPM, polling at its own expense in late September and early October, had the winner right and the lead 12.2 points short, with 18% undecided excluded. The two polls that had the wrong winner were the two with a party connection or an undisclosed commissioner: Faktor plus, five weeks out, missed by 25.5, and Ipsos, three days out with the largest sample and the only published margins of error, by 21.4.5,6,7,8 The pattern is therefore closer to Costa Rica 2018 (an independent poll short by 22 and a campaign-commissioned one short by 35) than to Britain 2015 (every firm short by the same 5–7), and it does not fit the Wisconsin 2020 pattern of one firm against an accurate field. What distinguishes Ipsos within the Serbian set is that it is the poll with the most recent fieldwork and the largest sample, and that only Faktor plus, five weeks out, had a larger error.

Venezuela presidential 2024 Official count disputed. Delphos/UCAB (5–11 Jul, n = 1,200) had González 59.1, Maduro 24.6; the CNE announced Maduro 51.95, González 43.18 without publishing precinct results, while the opposition’s tally sheets from 82% of polling stations gave González 67.1, Maduro 30.4. Against the CNE figure the margin error would be +43; against the tally sheets, −2. The Carter Center and the UN panel found the count did not meet basic standards of transparency, so the metric has no anchor. Excluded by rule (b).139,140
Georgia parliamentary 2024 Official count disputed. Edison Research for Formula TV (1–18 Oct, n = 1,200) had Georgian Dream 34 against 18 for the largest opposition list; the CEC counted 53.9 against 11.0 (margin error about −27). OSCE/ODIHR reported widespread intimidation and compromised secrecy in a quarter of observations, and Edison states the gap between its exit poll and the count cannot be explained by normal variation. Excluded by rule (b).136,137,138
Serbia 2026: NSPM (20 Oct) and Faktor plus (21 Sep) Fieldwork ended 20 and 35 days before the vote, outside rule (a); margin errors −12.2 and −25.5, reported in Section 3.5.
British Columbia 2013: Angus Reid (NDP 45, Liberals 36) Margin error −13.4, but the fieldwork dates could not be established from a primary source (the pollster’s own account refers to a final poll completed on 8 May); folded into the Ipsos Reid row.
Hungary 2022: Medián 49/41 Released on election day after the polls closed; not a pre-election publication. Medián’s last pre-election poll (50/40) is the row.
Alberta 2012: Forum 41/32 and Angus Reid 41/32 (21 Apr) Not the agencies’ final polls (Forum polled again on 22 Apr: 38/36); margin error −18.7 noted in the row.
US presidential 2016, national Not a miss: RCP average Clinton +3.2 vs actual +2.1 (error +1.1); the national polls were among the most accurate since 1936 (AAPOR 2017).
US presidential 2020, national Below threshold on the margin: AAPOR’s all-poll average overstated Biden by 3.9 points. The Wisconsin poll is the representative row.
US midterms 2022 (“red wave”) Not a miss on the national generic ballot: RCP R+2.5 and FiveThirtyEight R+1.2 vs actual R+2.7 (House popular vote, Clerk of the House). The “red wave” was a seat-expectation and partisan-pollster story, not a margin miss by the averages.
Poll-of-polls figures (UK 2015, Brexit, Argentina 2019) Averages are reported in the text but are not rows, since the catalogue compares named polls with published sample sizes.
Poland parliamentary 2015 Not a miss: final polls had PiS +6 to +16 (median ≈ 13) vs actual +13.5.
Spain April 2019 Not a miss on the margin: PSOE lead 11–12 in the final polls vs 12.0 actual.
France legislative 2024, 2nd round A seat-projection miss (RN projected first, NFP finished first), not a vote-share miss: RN and allies finished first in votes (37.1%); seat models are out of scope.
Italy 2013 Coalition-level final polls could not be retrieved from a primary or contemporaneous source; indicative margin error +6 to +8 only.
Austria presidential 2016 (May runoff and December re-run) Clear misses (Gallup/Österreich Hofer 53–47 vs Van der Bellen 50.35; December Hofer 52–48 vs Van der Bellen 53.8) but no sourced post-mortem was located, so the explanation column could not be filled to the standard used here.
New Zealand 2020 Final polls had Labour +15 vs actual +24.4 (error −9.4); winner obvious, no post-mortem located.
South Korea 2017 Realmeter’s last poll (Moon +23.8 over Hong) vs actual +17.0 (error +6.8), but the last polls were seven days old under the legal blackout and no post-mortem was located.
Ecuador 2021 runoff Mean of six final polls Arauz +0.2 vs Lasso +4.7 actual (error ≈ −4.9); borderline, and the pollster releases were not retrieved.
Malaysia 2018 The famous miss was Merdeka Center’s seat projection, not its vote share (PH +6 polled vs +12 actual, on a Peninsular-only sample); seat projections are out of scope.
Argentina general 2019; Slovakia 2023 (Focus); Czechia 2021 (Kantar); Scotland 2014 (Ipsos MORI); Spain 2023 (GAD3/Mediaset) Margin errors of 3.6–7 points from elections already represented by a larger miss by the same or another agency; not added as separate rows.
Jamaica 2016; Kenya 2017; Indonesia; Philippines Poll technical sheets could not be retrieved to the standard used here.

5 Caveats

  1. Selection. The catalogue is a list of well-documented failures, assembled from the post-mortem literature and a search of national cases in six languages, not a random sample of polls and not a census of misses: a miss in a country whose polling and results are poorly documented online will be missing here. It therefore says nothing about how often polls miss; Jennings & Wlezien’s 351-election dataset puts the typical final-week absolute error at about 2 points on a party’s share (they report no final-week figure for the margin).4 What it does allow is a like-for-like comparison of magnitudes among the misses that were large enough to be investigated.
  2. One poll per row. Choosing which final poll represents an election is a judgement, and the ranking below the top four depends on it: Publicus for Hungary 2022 (−19.7) or Forum’s 21 April poll for Alberta (−18.7) would move into ranks 6–8; Invamer for Colombia (−35.6) or Metron Analysis for Greece (−18.6) would not change the top. Where an agency published more than one final-week poll, the table uses the later one even when it missed by less (Alberta, Hungary). The caveat column gives the alternatives wherever the choice matters.
  3. Bases. Polls publish shares on different bases (decided voters, valid votes, two-party-preferred, seats, raw figures including undecided). The margin error is insensitive to which base is used as long as poll and result are on the same one; where a poll’s figures include an undecided share of u% and the result does not, the polled lead is understated by a factor of 1/(1−u), which for the rows concerned (Greece 2015, Alberta 2012, Argentina 2023, Bolivia 2020) moves E by one to two points — never enough to change a row’s position by more than one or two places, and never the top three. The table says which base each row uses; Israel’s seats are compared with seats, and the Serbian 2026 shares are on RIK’s all-ballots base, which Ipsos also used.
  4. Sample sizes. Two rows have no documented n and no z. The standardised error assumes simple random sampling with the published n. Real design effects (from weighting, clustering, or non-probability online recruitment) differ by pollster and mode and are not published, so every z here is an upper bound of unknown looseness, and rows whose z values are within a factor of about 1.5 of each other should not be read as ordered. The 2026 row is the one case where a design effect is applied, because Ipsos’s published intervals allow it to be backed out; that works in Ipsos’s favour.
  5. Secondary sources. Where an agency’s release is no longer online, the figures come from a contemporaneous report or a compiled table that cites it; each such case is marked in the table and in the reference. Four official results (Israel 2015, Hungary 2022, Peru 2021, Paraguay 2023) rest on documents reproducing the electoral authority’s figures because the authority’s own page could not be read. The Serbia 2012 poll rests entirely on media reports and is disputed by Ipsos.
  6. Explanations. The explanation column reports what inquiries, researchers, pollsters or journalists concluded about their case, labelled by type. Inquiry and academic findings carry more weight than pollster self-assessments, which carry more weight than press analyses. None of them is a finding about Serbia 2026.
  7. The 2026 result is RIK’s count from all 8,392 polling stations as read on 2 November 2026 (after the repeat voting of 1 November); RIK’s final report with absolute totals had not been published at that time. Re-enter the final figures in the data chunk and re-knit if they differ. The companion reports use RIK’s preliminary count of 31 October 2026 (8,339 of 8,392 stations; Studentska lista 53.03%, Ujedinjena Srbija 38.97%), which gives a margin error of −21.5 rather than −21.4; the difference does not change any conclusion or rank here.
  8. Self-citation. The companion report cited for the 2026 row is by the author of this document.

Every poll figure, official result and explanation in Table 1 cites one or more of the numbered entries below by superscript. Type labels: Poll (the agency’s release or a contemporaneous report of it), Result (electoral authority or a document reproducing its figures), Inquiry (official or industry post-mortem), Academic, Pollster (the agency’s own statement), Press, Analysis. All links were checked on 2 November 2026; where a site was unreachable at that time the entry says what was used instead.

Pollster · Fornoni, M. / Management & Fit (15 August 2019), iProfesional — Fernández underestimated by about seven points and Macri overestimated by about six; a “voto vergonzante” not disclosed to interviewers offered as part of the explanation. https://www.iprofesional.com/politica/297946-cambiemos-cristina-kirchner-elecciones-Por-que-las-encuestas-se-equivocaron-con-el-resultado-de-las-PASO
  109. Poll · AtlasIntel (4 August 2023). Encuesta Atlas – Argentina PASO 2023 — fieldwork 31 Jul–4 Aug, n = 9,517, online random digital recruitment, ±1: Juntos por el Cambio 31.9, Unión por la Patria 30.8, La Libertad Avanza 20.8, undecided 3.5, blank 1, null 1.4 (release PDF: cdn.atlasintel.org/922873a0-…pdf, linked from the poll page). https://atlasintel.org/poll/argentina-national-2023-08-04
  110. Result · Bloomberg Línea (31 August 2023). Resultados finales de las PASO — CNE escrutinio definitivo: LLA 29.86%, JxC 28.00%, UP 27.28% of valid votes incl. blank. https://www.bloomberglinea.com/2023/08/31/resultados-finales-de-las-paso-cuantos-votos-obtuvo-milei-y-la-diferencia-entre-bullrich-y-massa/

Ninguna encuesta pronosticó que Javier Milei obtendría el 30% de los votos: ¿por qué fallaron?, Chequeado — academics (Tagina, UNSAM; Tesio) cite very high non-response, non-probability online and phone samples, a large undecided bloc and a “voto vergüenza” for Milei; no poll had Milei above 24.5. https://chequeado.com/el-explicador/ninguna-encuesta-pronostico-que-javier-milei-obtendria-el-30-de-los-votos-por-que-fallaron/
  112. Poll · AtlasIntel (28 April 2023). Encuesta Atlas – Elecciones Paraguay 2023 — fieldwork 20–24 Apr, n = 2,320, online random digital recruitment, ±2: Alegre 34, Peña 33, Cubas 23, undecided 1.9 (all respondents). https://cdn.atlasintel.org/92d996fd-c862-4067-8b91-a7ea2e327fc5.pdf
  113. Result · ABC Color (26 May 2023). Los números definitivos de las elecciones — TSJE definitive count: Peña 1,291,209 (42.74%), Alegre 830,302 (27.48%), Cubas 692,429 of 3,021,069 votes; turnout 63.29%. The TSJE portal now serves only the 2026 municipal election; figures as reported from the TSJE proclamation (Última Hora, 25–26 May 2023). https://www.abc.com.py/politica/2023/05/26/los-numeros-definitivos-de-las-elecciones-asi-quedaron-los-votos/
  114. Press · La Nación (8 May 2023). La victoria de Santiago Peña reivindica la confianza hacia las encuestas — Atlas was the only poll departing from the consensus (Ati Snead 42.9/31.3, EcoDat 41.4/31.0, CBN 43.8/24.6); critics cite its online-only sample and questionnaire. https://www.lanacion.com.py/politica/2023/05/08/la-victoria-de-santiago-pena-reivindica-la-confianza-hacia-las-encuestas/
  115. Poll · Bloomberg Línea Brasil (1 October 2022). Datafolha: Lula mantém 50% dos votos válidos para o 1º turno e Bolsonaro, 36% — fieldwork 30 Sep–1 Oct, n = 12,800, face-to-face, 310 municipalities (TSE BR-00245/2022). https://www.bloomberglinea.com.br/2022/10/01/datafolha-lula-mantem-50-dos-votos-validos-para-o-1-turno-e-bolsonaro-36/

Result · Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (4 October 2022). 100% das seções totalizadas — Lula 57,259,504 (48.43% of valid votes), Bolsonaro 51,072,345 (43.20%), turnout 79.05%. https://www.tse.jus.br/comunicacao/noticias/2022/Outubro/100-das-secoes-totalizadas-confira-como-ficou-o-quadro-eleitoral-apos-o-1o-turno

Bolsonaro recebeu voto útil na última hora — a late “useful vote” from Ciro and Tebet to Bolsonaro in the final 24 hours judged very probable (13% had said they might switch); hostility to field teams; no methodological error acknowledged. https://www.bandab.com.br/politica/bolsonaro-recebeu-voto-util-na-ultima-hora-diz-datafolha/amp/

Onde as pesquisas podem ter errado — preliminary hypotheses: asymmetric abstention (Lula, Ciro and Tebet intenders turned out at lower rates than Bolsonaro intenders), shy voters, and outdated census sampling frames. https://fpabramo.org.br/2022/10/05/onde-as-pesquisas-podem-ter-errado

Summarised by Opalo, K. O., 15 Mar 2013 (kenopalo.com/2013/03/15). https://aceproject.org/ero-en/regions/africa/KE/kenya-post-election-analysis-iposos-2013

  134. Inquiry · Pennay, D. et al. / AMSRO Inquiry Panel (November 2020). Inquiry into the Performance of the Opinion Polls at the 2019 Australian Federal Election — a “polling failure”: samples over-represented the better educated and politically engaged and weighting did not correct it; the panel could not rule out herding because pollsters would not provide their data sets (Statistical Society of Australia summary: statsoc.org.au/News-and-media-releases/9356513; ABC News, 5 Apr 2022: abc.net.au/news/2022-04-05/election-2022-can-we-trust-opinion-polls-again/100965412). https://statsoc.org.au/News-and-media-releases/9356513
  135. Analysis · Bonham, K. (21 May 2019). The miracle is over: 2019 Australian federal election polling failure — 17 published final polls, combined sample about 23,600, two-party-preferred wrong by about three points, far outside combined sampling error; late swing and “shy Tory” rejected; self-herding possible. https://kevinbonham.blogspot.com/2019/05/the-miracle-is-over-2019-australian.html

Edison Research (1 Nov 2024) states the gap between its exit poll and the count cannot be explained by normal variation: ssrs.com/news/edison-research-2024-republic-of-georgia-exit-poll. https://cdn.osce.org/sites/default/files/f/documents/1/6/584029.pdf

UN Panel of Electoral Experts interim report, 9 Aug 2024: digitallibrary.un.org/record/4062104. https://cartercentee50c07c05.blob.core.windows.net/blobcartercentee50c07c05/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/venezuela-final-report-2025.pdf
